deep.reconstruction:
Folio 18r has no derivation. It is the outside (address side) of a folded letter cover that Gauss later reused as scrap paper. The writing is a French address in a hand other than Gauss's: "à Monsieur / Monsieur Gauss / à Gottingue." There is also a later archival shelfmark, "Math 13" with an older number "36/28" crossed out and the folio number (18) circled, and the library stamp of the Niedersächsische Staats- und Universitätsbibliothek Göttingen.

The only mathematical content is a small ink sketch near the top. It shows a tilted square (about 15–20° from the axes) with a dot marked at one corner. Around and inside it are isolated dots in a roughly 3×3 grid pattern.

Context matters for interpreting the sketch. The neighbouring pages work with Gaussian integers: biquadratic residue symbols such as (5+2i / 7) on the previous page, and linear substitutions and congruences in Z[i] on the next page. So the sketch is plausibly the standard geometric picture of a Gaussian-integer modulus. In that picture the multiples of a Gaussian integer m = a+bi form a square lattice in the plane, generated by the vectors (a,b) and (−b,a). One tilted fundamental square has area N(m) = a²+b², and the lattice points it contains form a complete residue system mod m. Gauss describes exactly this in Theoria residuorum biquadraticorum, Commentatio secunda (1832), §§ 39–46.

This reading is my conjecture, not stated on the page. If it is right, the drawn square would fit a small modulus such as 2+i (norm 5), whose side vector (2,1) is tilted against the integer grid. No numbers are written, so the modulus cannot be determined.

results.what: Possible sketch of a tilted fundamental square of the lattice of multiples of a Gaussian integer, drawn among integer lattice points (residue system modulo a complex modulus). This interpretation is conjectural.
results.modern_name: Fundamental domain of the ideal (m) in Z[i]; complete residue system modulo a Gaussian integer has N(m) elements
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss, Theoria residuorum biquadraticorum, Commentatio secunda (1832)

deep.surprise_reason: The page is an address cover with only an unlabelled doodle. Even under the most generous reading, the lattice-square picture of residues modulo a Gaussian integer is Gauss's own published idea from 1832.

checkable.asserts: The square spanned by (2,1) and (-1,2), i.e. by 2+i and i*(2+i), has area 5 = N(2+i). This is an illustrative guess at the modulus of the sketch.
Norm of 2+i is 5, so a complete residue system mod 2+i has 5 elements, matching the lattice points in one tilted fundamental square.

transcription_corrections: The transcription is essentially correct. 'à Monsieur / Monsieur Gauss / à Gottingue' is a French address in another hand, not mathematics by Gauss.
The sketch is a tilted square with a marked dot at one vertex and scattered dots roughly in a 3×3 pattern around and inside it; no numbers or labels accompany it.
'Math 13 [-36/28-] (18)' is archival foliation: an old number struck through and folio 18 circled, plus the library stamp. None of it is Gauss's writing.
